questions.problem: Which of the following is a schematic of the set ${A}^{2}$ for $A={x,y,z}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The set ${A}^{2}$ is equivalent to the Cartesian product ${A}^{2}=A\times A.$

The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

To create a schematic of the Cartesian product $A\times A$, we create a table and list the elements of the first set $A$ in a row across the top and the elements of the second set $A$ in a column down the left side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040355/assets/adaba1cfa0f8aaba7638c2b581bf90ce1146f3c6ce91fa79654652bf98a2c011.png)

Then, at each intersection, we write an ordered pair whose first coordinate is the corresponding element of the first set and the second coordinate is the corresponding element of the second set.

Our completed $A\times A$ schematic is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040355/assets/9150fac674c8ff0608996224022243ed1a218ce077e7ccd12e7e9c8b12b732c7.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Cardinality of a Cartesian Product
questions.problem: What is the cardinality of $C\times D$ for $C={0,1,2,...,11}$ and $D={s,t,u,v}?$
questions.worked_solution:
For any two finite sets $C$ and $D,$ the cardinality of $C\times D$ is

$$
|C\times D|=|C|\cdot |D|.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|C\times D| & =|C|\cdot |D| \\  & =12\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Cartesian Products With Three Sets
questions.problem:
If $A={-1,1}$ and $B={u,v},$ which of the following elements belong to $B\times B\times A?$

- $(v,v,1)$
- $((v,v),1)$
- $(1,v,u)$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B\times C$ consists of all ordered triples whose first coordinate belongs to $A,$ second coordinate belongs to $B,$ and third coordinate belongs to $C.$

In this case, $B\times B\times A$ consists of every combination of ${u,v}$ with ${u,v}$ and ${-1,1},$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}B\times B\times A={ & (u,u,-1),(u,u,1),(u,v,-1),(u,v,1), \\  & (v,u,-1),(v,u,1),(v,v,-1),(v,v,1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

$$
|B\times B\times A|=|B|\cdot |B|\cdot |A|=2\cdot 2\cdot 2=8.
$$

From the given options, we see that only $(v,v,1)\in B\times B\times A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

consists of every combination of $A\times B$ and $A,$ as shown in the schematic below.

$$
|A \times B| = |A| \cdot |B| = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

Now, the Cartesian product

$$
(A \times B) \times B
$$

consists of every combination of $A \times B$ and $B,$ as shown in the schematic below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040355/assets/5f4a74a98f9df15273d59131eadc1155ff2d1105e1027e7d10b7e2366102e046.png)

Note that 

$$
|(A \times B) \times B| = |A \times B| \cdot |B| = 4 \cdot 2 = 8.
$$

From the given options, we see that both $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}((p, 4), 9)}$ and $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}((q,9),4)}$ are in $(A \times B) \times B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
